source.title: A Geometric View for Understanding Concept Learning and Neuron Interpretation in Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Chen-Hao Zhang; Chris Lin; Su-In Lee

record.tranche_reason: The paper gives a specific conceptual refinement: it defines polysemanticity in terms of a neuron relating to multiple unrelated concepts, and argues that individual-neuron interpretation can be too coarse while multi-neuron units can give a more useful granularity. Its experiments measure synthetic concept-learning performance, not polysemantic-neuron prevalence or the versions’ specified behaviors.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses polysemanticity and presents synthetic SAE experiments, but the experiments report concept-learning F1 and concept-learning/neuron-interpretation disagreement rather than rates or activation patterns of neurons responding to unrelated inputs. The cited empirical claims about SAEs and polysemanticity are not results of this study. Rows below record related synthetic concept-learning outcomes as versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The study builds a set-theoretic framework for concept learning in SAEs and runs experiments on 2D synthetic clusters with ReLU and Top-K SAEs. It reports concept-learning F1 and disagreement ratios for selected SAE neuron sets. It never measures how often, or how strongly, neurons in a vision or language model respond to unrelated inputs. It also gives no causal test of superposition, initialization or architecture effects on polysemantic-neuron share. Its polysemanticity statements are definitions, cited claims, or constructive theorems, such as monosemanticity requiring at least as many neurons as concepts. None is an empirical result on any version. It is better placed as T6 (discusses without testing) than T5: it argues no version is wrong or needs restating with its own results.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially right. The authors frame concepts and SAE neuron regions as sets and derive geometric conditions and capacity bounds for single-neuron vs multi-neuron representation. They show on synthetic data that single neurons are often insufficient and that wider SAEs help. They conclude that concept learning and neuron interpretation need not agree, and call their empirical study of that link preliminary.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops a geometric and set-theoretic framework and evaluates trained ReLU and Top-K SAEs on two-dimensional synthetic concepts; it does not reproduce the original neuron-activation investigations.
record.method_sensitivity: In the synthetic experiments, concept-learning F1 and concept-learning/neuron-interpretation disagreement vary with concept overlap, task (separation versus approximation), SAE architecture, expansion factor, L0, and exact number of selected neurons. Exact-N F1 is not monotone in selected-neuron count.

fits_no_version.finding: In synthetic 2D data, single SAE neurons often fail to separate or approximate a concept. Example: ReLU SAE at L0=5 reaches F1 0.4144 with one neuron vs 0.8529 with a 4-neuron intersection. Perfect F1 with one neuron occurs only for a neuron-separable concept.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In SAEs on synthetic data, whether a single neuron can represent a concept depends on concept geometry; intersections of several neurons improve concept alignment.

fits_no_version.finding: Separation and approximation tasks give different F1 for the same concept (1.0 vs 0.9281). Choosing neurons by separation error can select units that miss the target concept almost entirely.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In synthetic SAE concept selection, the apparent quality of a neuron set depends on the learning objective and the selection metric.

fits_no_version.finding: The concept-learning/neuron-interpretation disagreement ratio falls with expansion factor, from 0.69 at EF=2 to 0.10 at EF=64. It is higher for overlapping than disjoint concepts and concentrated at intermediate F1 (Tables 1 and 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In synthetic SAEs, mismatch between concept-to-neuron and neuron-to-concept mappings shrinks with SAE width and grows with concept overlap.

record.problems: The empirical study is limited to two-dimensional synthetic clusters and trained ReLU and Top-K SAEs, so it does not measure polysemanticity prevalence in real vision or language models. Results are reported as best concept-learning metrics across seeds in the experiment details; uncertainty estimates for the reported F1 values are not stated. The authors describe their empirical study of concept-learning/neuron-interpretation disagreement as preliminary.
record.rows_left_out: No results were excluded that directly measure a version of the claim. The disagreement-ratio results in Table 1 and Table 2, and the width/sparsity sweeps in Figures 3 and 4, were not entered as claim-version rows because they measure concept-learning/neuron-interpretation disagreement or concept-learning capacity, not polysemantic-neuron prevalence. Cited results from other studies were also excluded.

untested.parts: No image classifier neurons are examined.
No transformer language-model MLP neurons are examined.
Only a theoretical capacity bound (d ≳ (kc!|C|)^{1/kc}) is given; there is no empirical test that superposition causes polysemanticity.
Initialization, regularization and noise as causes are not studied.
SAE width, sparsity and ReLU vs Top-K are varied, but the outcome is concept-learning F1 and disagreement, not the share of polysemantic neurons in a model.
Canonical polysemantic neurons in real networks are not revisited.

Metric choice (F1 vs separation error) changes which SAE neuron sets get selected for synthetic concepts. Polysemantic classification of neurons under different activation ranges or scoring choices is not tested.

missing.what: Disagreement ratio by expansion factor, concept type, task and architecture, and by F1 interval. Not tied to any version, but it is the paper's main quantitative result.

record.verdict_notes: All experiments are on 2D synthetic clusters with SAEs. 'Neurons' here are SAE features in a toy setting, not model MLP neurons. Results are best-across-seeds with no uncertainty reported. Statements that neurons are mostly polysemantic are cited from others (Templeton 2024; Elhage et al. 2022), not results of this study. Tranche changed from T5 to T6.

versions.untested_parts: No image classifier or natural-image neuron activations are measured.
No transformer language-model MLP neurons, tokens, or language contexts are measured.
The study gives theoretical capacity results but does not test whether superposition causes polysemanticity in trained networks.
Initialization, regularization, and training noise as causes of polysemanticity are not tested.

The study varies SAE architecture, expansion factor, and sparsity, but measures synthetic concept-learning scores and disagreement rather than the share of polysemantic neurons or performance costs of reducing that share.
It does not revisit canonical real-network neurons or test whether their mixed inputs share a feature the network uses.

The study compares concept-learning objectives and selection metrics, but does not test whether neuron polysemanticity classifications change with activation-range coverage or explanation-scoring choices.
